hero.text: The HSF Evidence Map brings together more than 53,000 studies on how health systems raise, pool and spend money. Explore what has been studied, where evidence is concentrated, how the field is changing, and which countries and health financing priorities remain underexplored.

funnel.label: — No abstract in any source (not screened)
Stage 1: Records entering the final selection
— Unsure at the September second-pass screening
— Included at the first pass, missing from the second pass
— Excluded: published before 2010 (no year at import)
— Financing function from the second-opinion check

gallery.title: Financing functions & outcomes
gallery.blurb: Explore which financing functions receive the most research attention and what outcomes the studies examine.

figs.title: Which financing functions are studied most?
figs.caption: Benefits decisions and purchasing have the most studies. A study may cover several financing functions.
technical_notes: Studies by financing function — a study can carry more than one. Benefits decisions leads at 13,088 studies, 1.1× Purchasing's 11,738; capital-investment financing trails furthest behind.
Base: 66,331 tags across 53,362 studies.

figs.title: How an extra classification check changes the results
figs.caption: Adding labels from the extra classification check changes each function’s share only slightly.
technical_notes: Share of studies tagged with each financing function: all included studies vs. excluding the studies whose label came from the second-opinion check. The largest change is for Revenue Raising: +1.1 percentage points when the 7,298 second-opinion studies are included.

7,298 studies had no function in the main panel; at least one of two second-opinion models found one. About 60% are expected to be genuine HFF studies (v2.2 README). A study can carry more than one function, so shares sum to more than 100%. Labels read: all studies / excluding second-opinion labels.

figs.title: What do the studies measure?
figs.caption: “Other” includes identifiable outcomes outside the eight named groups. A study may examine several outcomes.
technical_notes: Studies by outcome domain — a study can carry more than one. Other is tagged 4.6× as often as Equitable distribution of health system resources (28,726 vs 6,190), the next largest domain.
Base: 62,644 tags across 53,362 studies.

figs.title: Which outcomes are studied for each financing function?
figs.caption: Each row shows the outcomes examined by studies covering that financing function. Darker cells mean a larger share; shares can exceed 100%.
technical_notes: Outcome-domain mix of each financing function's tagged studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag of either kind, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 85% of Capital investment: other health system inputs studies report Other, its most common outcome.
Base: 53,362 studies; 'Unclear' tags excluded.

figs.title: How the financing functions studied have changed over time
figs.caption: Benefits decisions accounted for 27% of eligible studies at the start of the period and 24% at the end. A study may cover several functions.
technical_notes: Share of tagged studies by year, top 5 functions, shown as separate lines; a study can carry more than one, so totals can exceed 100%. Benefits decisions' share moved only from 27% to 24% across the whole period.
Base: 53,358 tags for the top 5 functions.

figs.title: How research on each financing function has grown
figs.caption: Financing-function assignments grew 1.9 times between 2010 and 2025. This counts functions assigned to studies, rather than unique studies.
technical_notes: Annual count of financing-function tags, by function (a study can carry more than one, so totals exceed the study count). Total tags grew 1.9× from 2010 to 2025; Benefits decisions's share moved from 22% to 19% of that total.
Base: 62,524 financing-function tags, 2010–2025 (2026 partial year omitted).

figs.title: How study methods, financing functions and outcomes overlap
figs.caption: Wider bands represent more studies. Each study is shown with one financing function and one outcome, selected from its recorded labels.
technical_notes: Each ribbon is a group of studies flowing from study design, through primary financing function, to primary outcome domain (first-listed tag of each). Ribbon width is the study count. Benefits decisions is the largest single financing-function node (10,552 studies), feeding most often into Other (22,334 studies primarily reporting it).

figs.title: What is included in “Other” outcomes?
figs.caption: Service use, access and coverage, and spending, prices and funding are the largest groups within “Other”.
technical_notes: Themes within the studies whose outcome domain is tagged 'Other'. Service use, access and coverage (29%) and levels, trends and drivers of spending, prices or funding (15%) are the largest themes.

Base: 28,726 studies with an 'Other' outcome; a study can carry two themes. For the September set, themes come from clustering the 'Other' justifications; for studies added in October, a language model assigned them (some themes exist only there). 6,827 studies (24%) fit no theme and are not shown.
figs.warning: 6,827 studies classified as Other could not be assigned a theme and are not shown. A study may appear in several themes.

figs.title: How the outcomes studied have changed over time
figs.caption: The share examining health improvement rose from 8% to 13%; financial protection rose from 7% to 9%, between 2010 and 2025.
technical_notes: Share of each year's studies investigating each named health-system goal, 2010-2025. Improved level/distribution of health rose from 8% to 13% and financial protection from 7% to 9%; the rest barely moved.

Base: 50,379 studies published 2010-2025; 2026 (partial year) excluded. Shares are of all studies that year, multi-label. Panels share the same y-axis, ordered by overall frequency. 'Other' and 'Unclear' are not shown.

gallery.title: Topic clusters
gallery.blurb: Explore groups of studies on similar subjects and the research fields they belong to.

figs.title: The 20 largest groups of research topics
figs.caption: The largest groups concern insurance programmes and medicines. Labels show characteristic words from each group.
technical_notes: Top 20 research themes, ranked by cluster size (keyword labels, not hand-assigned categories). 'medicaid / insurance / medicare' leads at 6,297 studies, 1.1× the next-largest ('drug / medicines / drugs', 5,654).
Base: 39,767 studies with a topic embedding, across 56 emergent themes.

figs.title: Groups of studies with similar topics
figs.caption: Each dot represents a study; nearby dots have more similar abstracts. This is a map of topics, not a geographic map.
technical_notes: Position uses a two-dimensional UMAP projection of abstract embeddings from the v2.4 topic model, coloured by HDBSCAN topic group or the share of single-country studies in lower-income countries. Projected distances are an approximation of abstract similarity.
Base: 53,362 studies with a topic embedding. Position = 2D UMAP projection of sentence embeddings; colour = HDBSCAN cluster.

figs.title: Which topic groups focus on lower-income countries?
figs.caption: Colours show how often each topic group’s single-country studies examine low- and middle-income countries.
technical_notes: Position uses a two-dimensional UMAP projection of abstract embeddings from the v2.4 topic model, coloured by HDBSCAN topic group or the share of single-country studies in lower-income countries. Projected distances are an approximation of abstract similarity.
Base: 42,413 single-country studies with a known income group and a topic embedding, across 57 emergent themes.

figs.title: Which research fields do the studies belong to?
figs.caption: Longer bars represent more studies in each research field. The fields come from publication metadata.
technical_notes: OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy - each radial bar is a subfield (length = studies), coloured by domain. 'Economics and Econometrics' leads at 11,820 studies, 2.4× the next-largest ('General Health Professions', 4,922); Social Sciences accounts for 21,907 of 41,967 studies with a topic label.
Base: 41,967 studies with an ml_thematic_cluster label (78.6% of the analysis population). Top 40 subfields shown, grouped and coloured by domain; shade reflects study count.

figs.title: Which research fields have the most studies?
figs.caption: Larger boxes represent more studies. Economics and Econometrics is the largest research field among studies with a field label.
technical_notes: Same OpenAlex-style topic taxonomy as the ranked chart, laid out as a treemap — each rectangle is a subfield (area = studies), grouped and coloured by field/domain. 'Economics and Econometrics' is 28% of 41,967 tagged studies on its own, 2.4× the next-largest subfield ('General Health Professions', 4,922) — proportional area makes that concentration immediately visible.

Base: top 12 subfields by study count (of 41,967 studies with an ml_thematic_cluster label). Cell area is directly proportional to study count; colour identifies the broader domain and shade reflects study count.

gallery.title: Disease focus
gallery.blurb: See which disease areas appear in the research and which financing functions are studied. These figures cover studies with disease classifications.

figs.title: Which disease areas are studied?
figs.caption: The figures cover studies assigned a disease category, rather than all studies in the map. Bar length shows the share in each disease area.
technical_notes: Each bar is a MeSH-derived disease category; length is its share of the disease-coded literature, colour is whether that research skews toward richer or poorer countries. Maternal & neonatal research skews most toward L&MICs (54% L&MICs); Injuries skews most toward high-income settings (93% high-income).
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

figs.title: Which financing functions are studied in each disease area?
figs.caption: Each row shows the financing functions covered by studies in that disease area. A study may cover several functions, so shares can exceed 100%.
technical_notes: Mix of financing-function tags within each MeSH-derived disease category (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). Injuries leans hardest on Pooling (49% of its tagged studies).
Base: 7,874 PubMed-MeSH-classified studies across 11 disease categories (partial coverage of the corpus).
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

figs.title: Which financing functions receive more attention in each disease area?
figs.caption: Blue cells show financing functions that are more common in a disease area than across disease-classified studies; red cells show functions that are less common.
technical_notes: For each MeSH-derived disease category, its share of tags for a given financing function, divided by that function's overall share across all disease-tagged studies. Blue = disproportionately more attention; red = disproportionately less. Skin studies are tagged Public financial management 2.8× as often as the disease-tagged average, while Neurological & mental studies are tagged Recurrent financing (supply chain) only 0.2× as often — the widest gaps in either direction.
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

figs.title: How the disease areas studied in lower-income countries have changed
figs.caption: Among disease-classified studies about low- and middle-income countries, non-communicable diseases became a larger share of research between 2010 and 2025.
technical_notes: Disease mix of MeSH-classified HFF research about low- and middle-income countries, across three epidemiological-transition classes. Communicable/maternal/nutritional fell 80%→51%; non-communicable rose 20%→46%, 2010–2025.
Base: 1,796 MeSH-classified studies about L&MICs. Shows the composition of research only; there is no disease-specific burden benchmark.
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

figs.title: How research about lower-income countries has changed by disease area
figs.caption: Dots show 2010–2017 and arrowheads show 2018–2026. An arrow to the right means a larger share of that disease area’s research concerns low- and middle-income countries.
technical_notes: Share of research about L&MICs within each MeSH-derived disease category, 2010–2017 (dot) to 2018–2026 (arrowhead). Skin's L&MICs share rose +19pp; Infectious's fell -10pp — the widest swings either way.

Base: PubMed-MeSH-classified, geo-tagged studies with a known country income group. The smallest category has 7 studies in one era, so read narrow categories with caution. Shows research share only, not a ratio to burden.
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

figs.title: Where each disease area has been studied
figs.caption: The maps show where studies in each disease area were identified. Darker colours mean more studies.
technical_notes: HFF studies naming each country, split by MeSH-derived disease area (busiest first). Log scale. 'Infectious' research reaches the widest set of countries (131 named); several disease areas stay concentrated in a handful of systems.
Base: 7,874 PubMed-MeSH-classified studies across 11 disease categories (partial coverage of the corpus; see README). Robinson projection.
figs.warning: Disease classifications are available for 7,874 of the 53,362 studies, so these figures describe a subset.

gallery.title: Methods & data
gallery.blurb: See how studies were designed, whether they used quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods, and what kinds of data they analysed.

figs.title: How the studies were carried out
figs.caption: Cross-sectional and correlational studies are the most common design. Routine administrative records are the most common data source.
technical_notes: Cross-sectional & correlational is the most common design (21%); cross-sectional data and administrative sources lead their dimensions (29% and 30%).
Note: Based on 53,362 studies. Each study was assigned one category per dimension (study design, data type and data source). Percentages may not sum to 100% due to rounding.
Unclear: no category could be assigned because the study's title and abstract did not give enough information to classify it confidently (the field was left blank at extraction).

gallery.title: Geographic coverage
gallery.blurb: Where health financing research is concentrated: which countries, income groups and settings it covers, how coverage has spread over time, and how methods vary by place.

figs.title: Where health financing research is focused
figs.caption: The map compares studies per 10 million people. Multi-country studies count in every country they cover.
technical_notes: HFF studies naming each country, per 10 million people (log scale), shown on a diverging red–blue scale. North America, Western Europe, Australia and the Gulf are studied far more intensively per capita than South Asia or sub-Saharan Africa — 54.8 studies per 10M people is the median.
Base: 182 countries with ≥1 study and population data. Grey = no study naming the country. Population: World Bank.

Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate. This map uses the country subset with disease-burden data, so Kosovo is omitted even though the displayed rate is based on population.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate. This map uses the country subset with disease-burden data, so Kosovo is omitted even though the displayed rate is based on population.

figs.title: The 20 countries with the most studies
figs.caption: The United States has the most studies in the map. Studies covering several countries count in each country.
technical_notes: Top 20 countries by study count — a multi-country study is counted once per country it names. United States of America leads with 15,487 study-country pairs, 4.4× China's 3,553.
Base: 47,650 study-country pairs across 184 countries.

figs.title: Research coverage by country income group
figs.caption: High-income countries account for the largest share of country coverage. A study counts once for each country it examines.
technical_notes: Each study counts once for every country it examines, grouped by the country's World Bank income level in the study's publication year. High income accounts for 30,121 pairs, ahead of Upper middle income's 9,382.
Base: 47,650 pairs; countries without an income group are excluded. Income group in the publication year (v2.2, gaps filled from the World Bank's historical classification).

figs.title: Which countries have more recent research?
figs.caption: Colour shows the share of a country’s studies published in 2018–2026. A higher share means more recent research, rather than necessarily faster growth.
technical_notes: Share of a country's HFF studies published in 2018–2026, the later half of the window (global average 61%). Green = more recent evidence base than average; brown = older. The share of recent studies is highest in the Gulf and parts of Africa; several Latin American and Eastern European countries still carry a majority pre-2018 evidence base.
Base: countries with ≥5 HFF studies, 2010–2026. Grey = fewer than 5 studies.

figs.title: The most common research approach in each country
figs.caption: Colour shows the most common analysis approach among each country’s studies. Countries with fewer than five studies are not classified.
technical_notes: The most common type of analysis among each country's HFF studies (≥5 studies). Colour is the modal category. Quantitative is the modal type in 133 of 164 countries with enough studies to classify — Qualitative leads in only 31.

gallery.title: Geographic inequalities
gallery.blurb: Compare how research is distributed with countries’ populations and disease burden. The comparisons highlight possible gaps among the studies identified by this map.

figs.title: Research coverage relative to health spending
figs.caption: Compare studies relative to health spending and explore the regional profiles. A high number of studies per dollar can reflect low spending, rather than a large research base.
technical_notes: Interactive page: HFF studies per US$1bn of total health expenditure by country, and a profile card for each WHO region (disease focus, top financing functions, financial protection as an outcome, country coverage over time). The African Region has the most studies per dollar spent (11.3 per US$1bn), because its health spending is so small, not because its evidence base is large. Places that the WHO's country list does not assign to a region (Taiwan, Hong Kong, Kosovo) take the WHO region of their UN M49 sub-region.

figs.title: Countries with high disease burden and little research in this map
figs.caption: The colours combine low, middle and high levels of disease burden and study counts. Red identifies countries with high burden and relatively few studies in this map.
technical_notes: Each country by its total disease burden (GBD 2023 DALYs) and its count of HFF studies naming it, in tertiles. Deep red = high burden, little research; blue = well-researched relative to burden; dark purple = high on both; cream = low on both. Angola, Algeria, Yemen, Uzbekistan, Venezuela fall in the highest-burden, lowest-evidence cell — top third globally for disease burden, bottom third for HFF research volume.
Burden: GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs (IHME), whole-country. Evidence: HFF studies naming the country. Robinson projection. 2 countries lack burden data (rendered grey).
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: Research relative to disease burden, by country
figs.caption: The map shows studies per 100,000 healthy years lost through illness or early death. Blue indicates more research relative to burden; red indicates less.
technical_notes: HFF studies naming each country, per 100,000 DALYs of disease burden. Blue: more research per unit of burden than the typical studied country; red: less. The median studied country has 1.63 studies per 100,000 DALYs — rich, small countries cluster far above that line, populous L&MICs far below it.
Base: 182 countries with GBD 2023 burden data and ≥1 study; global median 1.63. Grey = no study naming the country, or no GBD burden row.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: Countries with no studies identified in this map
figs.caption: Djibouti has disease-burden data but no included study naming it. This does not establish that no research exists there.
technical_notes: Countries by number of HFF studies naming them, against the whole map of GBD 2023 burden. Red = a country that carries disease burden but has no HFF study at all. Djibouti has GBD burden data but zero HFF studies naming it.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: How research coverage compares with disease burden
figs.caption: The middle-ranked high-income country has 15 times as many studies per unit of disease burden as the middle-ranked low-income country.
technical_notes: Each point is a country: research intensity (studies per unit of disease burden) against total burden. The median high-income country has 15× more HFF studies per 100,000 DALYs than the median low-income country.
Base: 182 countries with GBD 2023 burden data and ≥1 study. Point area ∝ population.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: How study counts compare with a disease-burden benchmark
figs.caption: This comparison asks what study counts would look like if countries’ research shares matched their shares of disease burden. It is an illustrative benchmark.
technical_notes: If research were proportional to disease burden, each country would hold a share of studies equal to its share of global DALYs. Bars right = below that expected count; left = above. India has about 6,647 fewer studies than a burden-proportional share; the largest surplus sits in United States of America (+13,391).
Expected = 47,565 study-country pairs × (country DALYs ÷ total DALYs). GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs (IHME).
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: Research share compared with disease-burden share
figs.caption: Countries below the comparison line have a smaller share of studies than their share of disease burden. This is a benchmark, rather than a recommended research allocation.
technical_notes: Each point is a country. Values below zero indicate a smaller share of HFF studies than the country's share of global disease burden. 96 of 182 countries have a smaller research share than burden share; 59% of these are low- or lower-middle-income.

Base: 182 countries with GBD 2023 burden data and ≥1 study; shares use this same country universe. GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs (IHME). Country research counts are study-country pairs: a multi-country study counts once per country. Equatorial Guinea and Djibouti have burden data but no identified studies and are not plotted. Horizontal markers show medians.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: Where research coverage is low relative to disease burden
figs.caption: The chart compares countries’ research shares with their shares of disease burden. The ranking depends on this benchmark and does not establish funding priorities.
technical_notes: This is an exploratory proportional-share benchmark, not a validated recommendation about funding or an estimate of the number of studies required. Country research share divided by disease-burden share. Zero on the log2 scale means proportional coverage; negative values indicate less research relative to burden. Eritrea has the largest finite relative gap: its research share is 64x smaller than its burden share. No identified studies: Djibouti.

Base: 183 countries with GBD 2023 burden data; 182 with ≥1 identified study are plotted and ranked. Both shares use this same 183-country universe. Country research counts are study-country pairs, so a multi-country study counts once per country. Points are equal size; population is not encoded.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: How the share of research about lower-income countries has changed
figs.caption: The share of single-country studies about low- and middle-income countries rose from 25% in 2010 to 41% in 2025.
technical_notes: Share of each year's single-country studies that are about low- and middle-income countries. It climbed from 25% in 2010 to 41% in 2025 — real progress, yet still far below the 83% of global disease burden L&MICs carry.

Base: single-country studies with a known income group, by publication year; 2026 (partial) omitted. Income group in the publication year (v2.2, gaps filled from the World Bank's historical classification). Burden reference: L&MICs share of GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate. Its studies can contribute to the research shares where eligible, but Kosovo is absent from the disease-burden benchmark.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate. Its studies can contribute to the research shares where eligible, but Kosovo is absent from the disease-burden benchmark.

figs.title: How research is concentrated across lower-income countries
figs.caption: Research is unevenly distributed across low- and middle-income countries. The five most-studied countries account for 46% of their evidence base.
technical_notes: Low- and middle-income countries ordered from least to most research per unit of disease burden. The five most-studied L&MICs hold 46% of the L&MICs evidence (Gini = 0.42).
Base: 124 L&MICs with GBD 2023 burden data.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: How research approaches and local authorship differ by income group
figs.caption: Research approach and the inclusion of locally based authors differ by country income group. These adjusted associations do not show cause and effect.
technical_notes: Adjusted odds ratios from two logistic models on single-country studies with a known income group. Reference group is high-income studies (OR=1). Adjusted for era; observational, so associations not causes. Low income studies have 0.40× the odds of a high-income study of using a quantitative analysis, and 0.07× the odds of high-income studies having a local author.
Base: 42,413 single-country studies with a known income group; 28,040 of these also have an author-affiliation country (local-authorship model).
figs.warning: The chart shows adjusted odds ratios, not probability ratios. Associations do not establish cause and effect.

gallery.title: Research ownership & collaboration
gallery.blurb: See where authors are based and how often teams include an author based in the country studied. Author locations do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: How often do studies include an author based in the country studied?
figs.caption: The map shows how often studies include at least one author based in the country studied. Author location refers to institutional affiliation, not nationality or leadership.
technical_notes: Share of a country's single-country HFF studies that have at least one author based there. Blue = a higher share with at least one locally based author; red = a lower share. North Korea has the lowest local-authorship share (0%) among countries with ≥5 studies with a known affiliation.
Base: 27,951 single-country studies with a known author-affiliation country, across 140 countries with ≥5 such studies.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: Where are authors of research about each income group based?
figs.caption: Among studies about low-income countries with author-location information, 19% have only locally based authors, 50% have mixed teams and 31% have no locally based author.
technical_notes: Author-affiliation pattern of single-country studies, by the income group studied. Only 19% of Low income studies have a local-only author team, and 31% have no local author at all.
Base: 28,040 single-country studies with a known income group and a recovered author-affiliation country.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: Local authorship by health financing function
figs.caption: The share including a locally based author ranges from 84% for the Overall category to 95% for Purchasing. These shares do not identify research leaders.
technical_notes: Share of single-country studies with a local author, by financing function tag. Only 84% of Overall studies have a local author, vs. 95% for Purchasing.

Base: single-country studies with a known income group, a recovered author-affiliation country, and >=1 financing-function tag; functions with <20 such studies excluded. A study can carry >1 function tag.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: Author-team locations by outcome studied
figs.caption: Each row shows where authors are based for studies examining that outcome. Mixed teams include authors based both inside and outside the country studied.
technical_notes: Authorship pattern of single-country studies reporting each outcome domain (row shares). Only 52% of Transparency and accountability studies have a local-only author team, the lowest share of any outcome domain.
Base: single-country studies with a known income group, a recovered author-affiliation country, and ≥1 outcome-domain tag. A study can carry >1 tag.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: Collaboration between authors in different income groups
figs.caption: Bands link income groups whose authors collaborate on the same studies. Wider bands mean more studies; within-group studies are excluded from the bands.
technical_notes: Cross-income co-authorship of 36,935 studies with a known author-affiliation country. Ribbons: studies co-authored across two income groups (within-group studies excluded from the ribbons). Most evidence isn't cross-income at all: 24,037 studies are wholly high-income-authored; just 225 wholly low-income.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research.

figs.title: Where studies include fewer authors based locally
figs.caption: Countries differ in the share of studies that include a locally based author. This measure alone does not establish local research capacity.
technical_notes: Each country by disease burden and the share of its studies with a local author. Niger: high burden, only 43% local authorship.
Base: 139 countries with ≥5 single-country studies with a known author-affiliation country. Local authorship is a proxy for research capacity, not its full measure.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Author locations are available for only part of the evidence base and do not establish who led the research. Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

gallery.title: Research funding
gallery.blurb: See which organisations are named as funders and which functions and outcomes their studies examine. Funder information is available for only part of the map.

figs.title: Which types of organisations fund the research?
figs.caption: Among studies that name a funder, 53% name national governments. A study may name more than one funder; these are study counts, not amounts of funding.
technical_notes: Share of studies naming each type of funder, among studies that report any funder. National governments fund 53% of funded studies; pharmaceutical companies 5.4% and other private companies 1.3%.

Base: 9,413 of 53,362 studies (17.6%) report a research funder (from CrossRef). Each named funder is assigned one type by keyword rules; a study naming funders of several types counts in each, so shares sum to >100%. National governments include ministries, national agencies, public research councils and bilateral aid agencies. Pharmaceutical companies include their corporate foundations.
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

figs.title: The most frequently named research funders
figs.caption: Larger boxes show funders named by more studies. Studies naming several funders count once for each.
technical_notes: Alternative view: the same top funders shown as a treemap after merging name variants into single entries. National Natural Science Foundation of China is named by 464 studies, more than any other funder.
Base: 9,495 of 53,362 studies (17.8%) name a funder; a study naming several funders counts once for each. Area shows funded studies; top 15 funders.
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

figs.title: Which financing functions appear in each funder’s studies?
figs.caption: Each row shows the share of that funder’s studies covering each financing function, among studies assigned a function. Shares can exceed 100% because functions overlap.
technical_notes: Each top funder's financing-function tag mix (share of that funder's studies with a financing function; a study can carry more than one tag). 40% of National Health and Medical Research Council's studies cover Benefits decisions, its most concentrated pairing among the top 12 funders.
Base: top 12 funders by study count, restricted to studies with ≥1 financing-function tag.
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

figs.title: Which outcomes are studied in each funder’s research?
figs.caption: Each row shows which outcomes are examined in that funder’s studies. It shows what was studied, rather than what the research found.
technical_notes: Outcome-domain mix of each top funder's studies (row shares; a study can carry more than one tag, so rows needn't sum to 100%). 77% of National Institute on Drug Abuse-funded studies report Other, its most common outcome.
Base: top 12 funders by study count, restricted to studies with ≥1 outcome-domain tag.
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

figs.title: How the funders named in studies have changed over time
figs.caption: The lines show each funder’s share of studies naming a funder in that year. They do not measure the amount of money provided.
technical_notes: Each top funder's share of that year's studies with a known funder, 2013–2025. National Natural Science Foundation of China's share rose +3.1pp from 2013–16 to 2022–25; Canadian Institutes of Health Research's fell -0.5pp.
Base: studies with a named funder; top 6 funders by total studies. 2026 (partial year) excluded.
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

figs.title: How funders, financing functions and author-team locations connect
figs.caption: Wider bands represent more studies connecting a funder, one recorded financing function and an author-team location. Only 535 eligible studies are shown.
technical_notes: Each ribbon is a group of single-funder, single-country studies flowing from research funder, through primary financing function, to authorship pattern. National Natural Science Foundation of China funds the most studies in this flow (154), and 30 of all 535 studies shown (6%) have no local author at all.
Base: 535 single-country studies with exactly one recognized funder (among the top 6 by study count), a known author-affiliation country, and ≥1 financing-function tag (primary tag shown).
figs.warning: Funder information is recorded for only part of the evidence base. Missing information does not mean a study had no funding.

gallery.title: Fragile & conflict-affected settings
gallery.blurb: How health financing research covers fragile and conflict-affected settings (FCAS): which countries carry the evidence, how it has grown, and how its outcomes compare with other income groups. Uses the World Bank FCAS list for each publication year.

figs.title: Countries affected by fragility or conflict with the most studies
figs.caption: Nigeria and Ethiopia appear in 38% of studies covering settings classified as affected by fragility or conflict. Multi-country studies may appear under several countries.
technical_notes: Studies about each fragile or conflict-affected country, top 20. 1,449 studies (2.7% of all) cover an FCAS country; Nigeria (361) and Ethiopia (191) appear in 38% of them.

Base: 1,449 of 53,362 studies name a country on the World Bank FCAS list in their publication year. A study covering several FCAS countries counts once per country. 54 FCAS countries appear in total. 'Multiple', 'Global' and region-level studies cannot be matched and are excluded; studies published after 2025 have no FCAS lookup (World Bank lists end there).

figs.title: How research in settings affected by fragility or conflict has changed
figs.caption: Research coverage increased. Part of the increase reflects changes in the World Bank country list; the fixed-country comparison also shows growth.
technical_notes: Studies on fragile or conflict-affected countries per year (top) and as a share of country-level studies (bottom). By each year's list the share tripled, 1.7% (2010-14) to 4.9% (2021-25); on a fixed set of countries it rose only from 4.5% to 6.5%.

Base: studies published 2010-2025 about at least one country with a World Bank income/FCAS lookup. Blue uses the World Bank FCAS list in each publication year. Grey counts, in every year, studies on any of the 54 countries listed at some point 2010-2025. Vertical lines mark the first year the largest study countries count as FCAS. 2026 is excluded (no lookup yet).

figs.title: Which outcomes are studied in settings affected by fragility or conflict?
figs.caption: Compared with studies about high-income countries, studies in these settings more often examine financial protection and less often examine resource use.
technical_notes: Share of studies in each setting that investigate each health-system goal. Versus high-income settings, FCAS studies focus more on financial protection (12% vs 6%) and less on efficiency in resource use (8% vs 13%).

Base: studies with a World Bank country lookup; each column is the share of that group's studies tagged with the goal (multi-label). FCAS overlaps the income columns (most FCAS countries are low or lower-middle income). A study covering countries in several income groups counts in each. Income group is taken in the publication year; 'Upper-middle' is the source file's 'MIC' code.

gallery.title: The financing backdrop
gallery.blurb: Explore how international health aid and spending per person have changed. Dashed lines show forecasts.

figs.title: How international aid for health has changed
figs.caption: International health aid fell from its 2021 peak. The 2025 estimate is preliminary; dashed lines show forecasts for 2026–2030.
technical_notes: Development assistance for health (DAH), 1990–2030 — solid is historical/preliminary, dashed is forecast. DAH fell 51% from its 2021 peak ($80bn) to $39bn in 2025, and is forecast to stay flat through 2030.
Base: IHME Financing Global Health 2025. 2025 is preliminary; 2026–2030 is forecast.

figs.title: Which donors reduced health aid in 2025?
figs.caption: The United States accounts for the largest reduction shown, at $9.5 billion. The net decline across all sources is $11.0 billion; 2025 estimates are preliminary.
technical_notes: Change in development assistance for health by source, 2024 → 2025. The US cut $9.5bn (-66%); compared with the $11.0bn net drop across all sources combined.
Base: IHME Financing Global Health 2025, DAH by source, 2023 USD millions converted to billions.

figs.title: How health spending per person differs by country income group
figs.caption: Average health spending per person is much higher in high-income countries. Dashed lines show forecasts; dollar amounts are expressed in 2023 prices.
technical_notes: Total health spending per person by World Bank income group, 2000–2030 (log scale; dashed = forecast). By 2025, the average person in a high-income country has $7,006 spent on their health — 174× the $40 in a low-income country, where per-person spending has fallen since 2020 ($52).
Base: IHME Financing Global Health 2025, health spending per person by World Bank income group. 2025–2030 are forecast.

gallery.title: Where financing and evidence diverge
gallery.blurb: Compare research coverage with health spending and disease burden. These exploratory comparisons do not estimate how much research or funding a country needs.

figs.title: How regional shares of health aid and research compare
figs.caption: Sub-Saharan Africa receives 53% of health aid but accounts for 10% of study-country counts. These are different measures and need not have matching shares.
technical_notes: Share of global DAH (2022–24 average) vs. share of HFF study-country pairs, by region (IHME GBD super-regions, approximated by income group then UN sub-region; not WHO regions). Sub-Saharan Africa receives 53% of DAH but only 10% of study-country pairs — the largest aid-to-evidence gap of any region.

Regions here are IHME's GBD super-regions, not the WHO regions used elsewhere on this site, so that study counts can be set against IHME's aid data. Base: IHME DAH by GBD super-region. Countries are grouped by World Bank income group, then UN M49 sub-region, which approximates (but does not exactly match) IHME's super-regions.

figs.title: How health spending and research coverage are related
figs.caption: Countries spending more on health per person tend to have more studies per person. This association does not show that spending causes more research.
technical_notes: Studies per million people vs. health spending per person (2025), by country. Log-log correlation r=0.63 across 179 matched countries — richer-spending countries are studied far more intensively per capita.
Base: 179 countries with IHME health-spending data (2025), World Bank population and at least one study.

figs.title: Research coverage compared with disease burden and health spending
figs.caption: This exploratory comparison combines disease burden, health spending and research coverage. Its rankings depend on how the comparison benchmark is defined.
technical_notes: This is an exploratory proportional-share benchmark, not a validated recommendation about funding or an estimate of the number of studies required. Disease burden vs. total health expenditure (left, shaded below the burden-proportional spending line); bubble size is each country's number of HFF studies, so a small bubble below the line is both below the spending and research comparison lines. The 15 countries with the largest shortfall once burden AND spending capacity are both counted (right). Eritrea alone is 5,233 studies short of a share proportional to its burden-to-spending benchmark — the largest gap of any country.

Base: 180 countries matched across GBD 2023 DALYs, IHME health spending per person × World Bank population (2025), and study-country pairs. Point area ∝ number of HFF studies. Need index = (country's share of total burden) ÷ (country's share of total spending); expected = total studies × (country need index ÷ sum of all need indices). Dashed line = spending exactly proportional to burden, i.e. every country spending the same amount per DALY.
Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.
figs.warning: Kosovo has 8 included studies but no comparable GBD 2023 DALY estimate, so it is excluded from this figure, which requires disease-burden data.

figs.title: Research coverage compared with health spending
figs.caption: This chart compares research coverage with health spending. A gap against spending is different from a gap against disease burden and does not establish a funding priority.
technical_notes: This is an exploratory proportional-share benchmark, not a validated recommendation about funding or an estimate of the number of studies required. Where research is most sparse relative to health spending (left, shaded), and the 15 countries with the largest absolute shortfall (right). United States of America alone is 5,835 studies short of a spending-proportional share — the largest gap of any country.

Base: 180 countries matched between IHME health spending per person × World Bank population (2025) and study-country pairs. Point area ∝ population. Expected = studies × (country expenditure ÷ total expenditure). Priority zone/reference line use the median rate as a descriptive split, not a proportionality claim (unlike the disease-burden scorecard). This flags countries under-studied relative to money spent, not necessarily neglected relative to need — so, unlike the disease-burden scorecard, high-spending wealthy countries can top this list alongside (or instead of) under-resourced ones.

gallery.title: How research priorities differ
gallery.blurb: How the financing functions and outcomes that research focuses on differ between countries that spend more or less on health.

figs.title: How financing functions differ between lower- and higher-spending countries
figs.caption: Benefits decisions take a larger share of financing-function assignments in higher-spending country groups. The four groups are based on health spending, not country income.
technical_notes: Financing-function mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Benefits decisions's share rises +9.2pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Revenue Raising's share falls -8.6pp.
Base: 166 countries split into spending quartiles (IHME, 2025); shares are quartile averages, renormalized to 100%.

figs.title: How outcomes studied differ between lower- and higher-spending countries
figs.caption: Resource-use outcomes take a larger share in higher-spending country groups. These are normalised category shares, rather than percentages of unique studies.
technical_notes: Outcome-domain mix (% of classified research) by health-spending quartile. Efficiency in resource use's share rises +3.8pp from the lowest- to highest-spending quartile, while Quality of service provision's share falls -3.9pp.
Base: 159 countries split into spending quartiles (IHME, 2025); shares are quartile averages, renormalized to 100%.

figs.title: How each financing function relates to health spending
figs.caption: Each dot is a country. The small charts show how research shares vary with spending per person; fitted lines show associations, not effects.
technical_notes: Each function's share of a country's classified research vs. health spending per person (log x-axis), one panel per function, with a linear trend line. Benefits decisions's share rises most with spending (r=0.37); Recurrent financing for the procurement and distribution of supply chain inputs's share falls most (r=-0.28).

figs.title: Which financing functions are more common in higher-spending countries?
figs.caption: Positive values mean a function is more common in countries spending more per person; negative values mean it is less common. These associations do not establish cause and effect.
technical_notes: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.37; Recurrent financing for the procurement and distribution of supply chain inputs correlates at r=-0.28, a negative association.
Base: 166 countries with ≥5 classified financing-function tags matched to IHME health spending per person (2025).

gallery.title: How research responds over time
gallery.blurb: Compare trends in research and international health aid. Similar trends do not establish cause and effect.

figs.title: How health financing research and international health aid changed over time
figs.caption: Lines compare changes from the 2010–2011 starting level, set to 100. Similar trends do not show that changes in aid caused changes in research.
technical_notes: Growth index (2010–2011=100) for the 6 largest financing functions' study counts, vs. global DAH, 2010–2025. Revenue Raising correlates with the DAH trend at r=0.64, the closest match among the 6 largest financing functions.
Base: financing-function tags by publication year, 2010–2025, vs. IHME DAH for the same years. Each series indexed to its own 2010–2011 average.

figs.title: Research on raising health funds alongside international aid
figs.caption: The chart places research on raising health funds alongside international health aid. The two lines use different vertical scales and do not establish a causal relationship.
technical_notes: Studies tagged Revenue Raising per year (this dataset) vs. global DAH (IHME), 2010–2025. Revenue-Raising research volume tracks the real DAH trend (correlation r=0.64) — both rose through the 2010s and have pulled back since the DAH peak.
Base: 7,885 Revenue-Raising-tagged studies, 2010–2025, vs. IHME DAH for the same years.

figs.title: How the ranking of financing functions changed between two periods
figs.caption: Compare the ranking of functions by average annual study count in 2015–2019 and 2022–2025. Rank 1 means the most studies.
technical_notes: Rank of each function's average annual study count, DAH boom era (2015–2019) vs. bust era (2022–2025). Public financial management climbed from rank 5 to 4; Overall fell from rank 6 to 7.
Eras chosen around the 2020–21 COVID-19 spike in development assistance for health (IHME).

gallery.title: USA sensitivity analysis
gallery.blurb: See whether the patterns change when studies about the United States are left out.

figs.title: Research–spending relationships after excluding US studies
figs.caption: This repeats the research–spending comparison after removing studies about the United States. Studies are removed by country studied, not author location.
technical_notes: Correlation between each function's share of a country's research and log(health spending per person), across countries. Studies mapped to the United States of America are excluded before country shares are recalculated. Benefits decisions correlates at r=0.38; Recurrent financing for the procurement and distribution of supply chain inputs correlates at r=-0.27, a negative association.
Base: 165 countries with ≥5 classified financing-function tags matched to IHME health spending per person (2025); USA-mapped studies excluded.

figs.title: Do the research–spending patterns change without US studies?
figs.caption: The two sets of dots compare the full dataset with the dataset excluding studies about the United States. The pattern changes little.
technical_notes: Paired lollipops compare each financing function's correlation between country-level research share and log(health spending per person): all studies versus the no-USA sensitivity analysis. The largest shift is for Pooling (-0.03 to -0.07).
Base: all-studies version uses 166 countries; no-USA version uses 165 countries.

figs.title: How research–spending relationships change without US studies
figs.caption: The two sets of dots compare associations before and after removing studies about the United States. They do not measure causal effects.
technical_notes: Each point compares the correlation between a financing function's country-level research share and log(health spending per person) before and after removing all studies mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Pooling (-0.03 to -0.07).
Base: all-studies version uses 166 countries; no-USA version uses 165 countries. Numbers at right show the change in r.

figs.title: How the financing functions studied change without US studies
figs.caption: The chart compares shares of financing-function assignments with and without studies about the United States. A study may have several function assignments.
technical_notes: Each point compares a financing function's share of all classified function tags in the full dataset versus after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. The largest shift is for Pooling (-4.3 percentage points).
Base: 66,331 classified financing-function tags overall; 15,487 studies mapped to the United States of America were removed before recalculating the comparison distribution.

figs.title: Which function shares change after excluding US studies?
figs.caption: Pooling shows the largest change, a decline of 4.3 percentage points in its share of financing-function assignments.
technical_notes: Percentage-point change in each function's share of all classified function tags after removing every study mapped to the United States of America. Pooling changes the most (-4.3 percentage points), showing how small the overall composition shift is.
Base: 66,331 classified financing-function tags overall; 15,487 USA-mapped studies removed.

gallery.title: Open access & author countries
gallery.blurb: See how often studies are free to read and where their authors are based. Access status could be checked only for studies with a DOI.

figs.title: How often studies by authors in each country are free to read
figs.caption: The map shows the share of checked studies that are free to read, for studies with at least one author based in each country.
technical_notes: Open-access share of studies with at least one author based in each country. Blue = more open access than the average study; red = less. 93 of 108 author countries beat the average study (65%), which the large US output (61% open) pulls down. Among countries with ≥200 studies, Uganda is highest (89%) and Turkey lowest (56%).

Base: 35,259 studies with a DOI and known author-affiliation countries (open-access status and affiliations from OpenAlex), across the 108 author countries with ≥20 studies (others grey). A study counts once for every country its authors are based in.
figs.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

figs.title: How the share of studies free to read has grown
figs.caption: Among studies whose access status could be checked, the share free to read rose from 39% in 2010 to 74% in 2025.
technical_notes: Share of each year's studies (with a DOI) that are open access. It rose from 39% in 2010 to 74% in 2025, passing half in 2013.

Base: 39,446 studies published 2010-2025 with a DOI; open-access status from OpenAlex, looked up on the DOI. 11,239 studies without a DOI are excluded because their status can't be checked. 2026 is excluded as a part year.
figs.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

figs.title: How free access differs by author-team location
figs.caption: Studies with authors based in low- and middle-income countries are more often free to read. “Mixed” teams include authors based in both high-income and lower-income countries.
technical_notes: Open-access share by where a study's authors are based (dashed line: all studies). 71% of L&MICs-only author teams publish open access and 77% of mixed teams, vs 61% of teams based only in high-income countries.

Base: 35,186 studies with a DOI whose author countries all have an income group in the site's country reference (OpenAlex). Left: a study counts in every income group its authors come from. L&MICs = low- and middle-income. 73 studies with an author in a country missing from the reference (e.g. Taiwan, Israel) are left out.
figs.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.

figs.title: Free access among studies with authors based in each country
figs.caption: The chart compares free access among studies with authors based in each of the 25 most active author countries. A study can count in several countries.
technical_notes: Open-access share of studies with at least one author based in each country, the 25 most active author countries. Iran tops the list (81%) and Taiwan is lowest (60%); the average is 76% across middle/low-income author countries vs 70% across high-income ones.

Base: 35,259 studies with a DOI and known author-affiliation countries (OpenAlex). A study counts once for every country its authors are based in. Countries shown: the 25 with the most studies (each ≥100). Income group is the site's country reference (current World Bank group).
figs.warning: Access status was checked using DOI identifiers. Studies without a DOI could not be checked.
